title: Microbiology Paper 1: General Microbiology and Infection Control
source: Adapted from user-provided IPI Microbiology assessments and question banks

objective.question: The ability of a microorganism to cause disease is called:
objective.explanation: Virulence is the degree of pathogenicity or capacity to cause disease. A pathogen is the disease-causing organism itself.

objective.question: In the five-kingdom classification system, bacteria were traditionally placed in the kingdom:
objective.explanation: The historical five-kingdom system placed prokaryotes in Monera. Modern classification uses domains and does not treat viruses as a kingdom.

objective.question: Which organism is a common cause of dental caries?
objective.explanation: Streptococcus mutans is strongly associated with dental plaque and caries; lactobacilli can contribute to lesion progression.

objective.question: Which reagent is not part of the Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast staining procedure?
objective.explanation: Ziehl-Neelsen staining uses carbol fuchsin, heat, acid-alcohol and a counterstain such as methylene blue. Iodine is used in Gram staining.

objective.question: A facultative anaerobe is an organism that:
options: Can grow with or without oxygen, usually growing better when oxygen is available
objective.explanation: Facultative anaerobes use oxygen when available but can switch to anaerobic metabolism when it is absent.

objective.question: Which Plasmodium stage is found inside red blood cells and develops into a replicating schizont?
objective.explanation: Merozoites invade red cells and develop through ring/trophozoite stages into schizonts; gametocytes also circulate inside red cells but are not the replicating erythrocytic schizont stage.

objective.question: Which method reliably sterilises heat-stable instruments and destroys bacterial endospores?
objective.explanation: Validated moist-heat autoclaving under pressure is a standard method for sterilising heat-stable instruments and destroying endospores.

objective.question: Which statement about the vaccination threshold needed for herd protection is most accurate?
options: It varies by pathogen and population; there is no universal percentage
objective.explanation: The required immunity threshold depends on transmissibility, vaccine effectiveness and mixing patterns; fixed percentages are not universal.

objective.question: Which virus is a common cause of acute diarrhoea in young children?
objective.explanation: Rotavirus is an important cause of severe acute gastroenteritis in young children.

objective.question: Oral hairy leukoplakia is associated with:
objective.explanation: Oral hairy leukoplakia is associated with Epstein-Barr virus, especially in immunocompromised patients.

objective.question: Candida albicans, a common cause of oral thrush, is classified as a:
objective.explanation: Candida albicans is a yeast-like fungus that can also form pseudohyphae and true hyphae under some conditions.

objective.question: Which method can reliably destroy bacteria including their endospores on heat-stable items?
objective.explanation: Autoclaving is validated moist-heat sterilisation that destroys bacterial endospores when correct time, temperature and pressure are achieved.

objective.question: A major function of IgG is to:
options: Mediate immediate allergy as the principal antibody
Neutralise toxins and pathogens and opsonise microbes
objective.explanation: IgG neutralises toxins and viruses, opsonises organisms and participates in complement activation. IgE is the principal antibody in immediate allergic reactions.

objective.question: Most potentially self-reactive T-cell clones are eliminated during development in the:
objective.explanation: Negative selection of developing T cells occurs primarily in the thymus. B-cell central tolerance occurs mainly in bone marrow.

objective.question: Artificially acquired passive immunity results from:
options: Exposure to an antigen followed by one's own antibody response
Transfer or injection of preformed antibodies
objective.explanation: Artificial passive immunity is produced by administering preformed antibodies, such as immunoglobulin or antitoxin.

objective.question: The type of immunity present from birth is primarily:
objective.explanation: Innate immunity is present from birth and includes physical barriers, innate immune cells and soluble factors.

objective.question: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria in the genus:
objective.explanation: Tuberculosis is caused mainly by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacterium with a mycolic-acid-rich cell wall.

objective.question: True or false: Most bacteria have a single main chromosome rather than paired homologous chromosomes.
objective.explanation: True. Most bacteria are haploid and have one main chromosome, although exceptions and additional plasmids occur.

objective.question: True or false: A parasite living inside a host is called an ectoparasite.
objective.explanation: False. A parasite living inside its host is an endoparasite; an ectoparasite lives on the host's surface.

objective.question: True or false: Staphylococcus species can cause dysentery and are the usual cause of dental abscesses.
objective.explanation: False. Dysentery is commonly caused by organisms such as Shigella or Entamoeba histolytica. Dental abscesses are usually polymicrobial, often involving oral streptococci and anaerobes; Staphylococcus is not the usual cause.

structured.question: Outline four characteristics of hospital-acquired (healthcare-associated) infections.
markingGuide: Acquired during healthcare delivery and not present/incubating at admission: 3 marks.
May become apparent during admission or after discharge within the relevant surveillance period: 2 marks.
Associated with procedures, devices, healthcare exposure or cross-transmission: 3 marks.
Can involve antimicrobial-resistant organisms and cause increased morbidity, length of stay or cost: 2 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: A healthcare-associated infection is acquired as a result of receiving healthcare and was not present or incubating at the time of admission. It may become evident during care or after discharge, depending on the infection and surveillance definition. Risks include surgery, invasive devices, antimicrobial exposure, contaminated environments and transmission between patients or staff. Such infections can involve resistant organisms and increase morbidity, length of stay and cost.

structured.question: (a) Name four major groups of protozoa and give one example each. (b) Name four clinical classes of mycoses. (c) List four common sources/reservoirs of infection.
markingGuide: Protozoa groups such as amoebae, flagellates, ciliates and apicomplexans/sporozoa with examples: 8 marks.
Superficial, cutaneous, subcutaneous and systemic/deep mycoses (opportunistic may be discussed): 4 marks.
Any four sources/reservoirs, e.g. humans, animals, soil, water, food, fomites or endogenous flora: 4 marks.
Clear examples/locations: 4 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: Traditional protozoan groupings include amoebae (Entamoeba histolytica), flagellates (Giardia duodenalis or Trypanosoma), ciliates (Balantidium coli) and apicomplexans/sporozoa (Plasmodium). Clinical mycoses are commonly classified as superficial, cutaneous, subcutaneous and systemic/deep; opportunistic mycoses are also recognised. Infection sources/reservoirs include infected or colonised humans, animals, soil, water, contaminated food and fomites; endogenous normal flora may cause opportunistic infection.

structured.question: List four classes of antimicrobial agents and explain how to distinguish sterilisation, disinfection and antisepsis. Give four sterilisation methods and four effects of heat on microorganisms.
markingGuide: Four antimicrobial classes, e.g. antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal, antiparasitic: 4 marks.
Correctly distinguishes sterilisation, disinfection and antisepsis: 6 marks.
Four methods such as moist heat/autoclave, dry heat, filtration, radiation or gas sterilisation: 4 marks.
Four heat effects, e.g. protein denaturation, membrane damage, enzyme inactivation and nucleic-acid damage: 4 marks.
Notes appropriate application/safety: 2 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: Antimicrobial agents include antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic drugs. Sterilisation destroys or removes all forms of microbial life, including endospores. Disinfection reduces or destroys many pathogenic microorganisms on inanimate objects but may not destroy spores. Antisepsis uses antimicrobial chemicals on living tissue. Sterilisation methods include moist heat (autoclaving), dry heat, filtration, ionising radiation and validated gas sterilisation such as ethylene oxide. Heat damages microorganisms by denaturing proteins, inactivating enzymes, disrupting membranes and damaging nucleic acids.

structured.question: (a) Describe the bacterial growth curve. (b) Classify bacteria according to morphology and arrangement. (c) Name five bacteria and give one characteristic for each.
markingGuide: Lag, log/exponential, stationary and death/decline phases with explanation: 8 marks.
Cocci, bacilli, vibrios, spirilla/spirochaetes; arrangements such as diplo-, strepto- and staphylo-: 6 marks.
Five accurate organism/feature pairs: 5 marks.
Terminology clarity: 1 mark.
structured.modelAnswer: In a closed culture, the lag phase is adjustment with little cell division; the log phase has rapid exponential growth; the stationary phase has growth balanced by death as nutrients decline and waste accumulates; and the death phase has viable numbers falling. Morphologies include cocci, bacilli, curved vibrios, spirilla and spirochaetes. Arrangements include pairs (diplo-), chains (strepto-), clusters (staphylo-) and packets. Examples: Staphylococcus aureus—Gram-positive cocci in clusters; Streptococcus pyogenes—Gram-positive cocci in chains; Escherichia coli—Gram-negative rod; Vibrio cholerae—curved Gram-negative rod; Mycobacterium tuberculosis—acid-fast bacillus with mycolic acids.

structured.question: (a) Explain Koch's postulates. (b) Describe Gram staining and explain the difference in Gram-positive and Gram-negative staining. (c) Describe the key structure of a bacterial cell.
markingGuide: States classic postulates: organism associated with disease, isolated in pure culture, causes disease in susceptible host, re-isolated: 6 marks.
Correct Gram-stain sequence: crystal violet, iodine, decolouriser, counterstain: 5 marks.
Explains thick peptidoglycan retains crystal-violet iodine complex; Gram-negative decolourises and counterstains: 4 marks.
Bacterial cell structures and functions: nucleoid, ribosomes, membrane, wall, capsule, plasmids, flagella/pili: 5 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: Classic Koch's postulates state that a suspected pathogen should be associated with disease, isolated and grown in pure culture, cause a similar disease in a susceptible host when introduced, and be re-isolated from that host. In Gram staining, crystal violet is the primary stain, iodine is the mordant, alcohol/acetone is the decolouriser and safranin is the counterstain. Gram-positive bacteria retain the crystal-violet–iodine complex because of thick peptidoglycan and appear purple; Gram-negative bacteria are decolourised and take the counterstain, appearing pink/red, due to their thinner peptidoglycan and outer membrane. A bacterial cell has a plasma membrane, usually a peptidoglycan wall, cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes and a nucleoid; some have plasmids, capsules, flagella, pili and endospores.

structured.question: (a) Explain how fungi are classified and outline the four clinical classes of mycoses with location and example. (b) State general fungal characteristics. (c) Give six roles of normal flora and four uses of microorganisms.
markingGuide: Explains fungal morphology/yeast, mould and dimorphic classification: 3 marks.
Superficial, cutaneous, subcutaneous and systemic mycoses with sites and examples: 8 marks.
General fungal features: eukaryotic, chitin/glucan wall, ergosterol membrane, yeast/hyphal forms: 3 marks.
Six normal-flora roles: colonisation resistance, vitamin production, immune development, metabolism, etc.: 3 marks.
Four beneficial uses of microbes: food fermentation, medicines, biotechnology, waste treatment, agriculture: 3 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: Fungi are eukaryotes with chitin- and glucan-containing walls and ergosterol-containing membranes. They occur as unicellular yeasts, filamentous moulds with hyphae/mycelium, or dimorphic forms that change with environment. Superficial mycoses affect outer stratum corneum or hair (e.g. pityriasis versicolor); cutaneous mycoses affect keratinised skin, hair or nails (dermatophyte tinea); subcutaneous mycoses involve dermis/subcutaneous tissue after traumatic inoculation (e.g. sporotrichosis); systemic/deep mycoses involve internal organs, often after inhalation (e.g. histoplasmosis). Normal flora provide colonisation resistance, produce some vitamins, support immune maturation, aid digestion/metabolism, maintain local conditions and may supply useful metabolites. Microorganisms are used in food fermentation, antibiotic/enzyme production, biotechnology and genetic engineering, agriculture, bioremediation and wastewater treatment.

structured.question: (a) Describe malaria parasite life-cycle stages in humans and mosquitoes, distinguishing pre-erythrocytic and erythrocytic phases. (b) Give prevention measures. (c) Define parasite and describe parasitic relationships, parasite types and host types.
markingGuide: Mosquito inoculates sporozoites; liver stage forms hepatic schizonts/merozoites: 4 marks.
Erythrocytic cycle: invasion, ring/trophozoite, schizont, RBC rupture; gametocytes: 4 marks.
Mosquito sexual cycle and sporozoite migration: 2 marks.
Four appropriate prevention measures: 4 marks.
Defines parasite and describes relationships/types/hosts with examples: 6 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: An infected female Anopheles mosquito inoculates Plasmodium sporozoites, which enter hepatocytes and undergo pre-erythrocytic schizogony to release merozoites. Merozoites invade red cells and develop through ring/trophozoite and schizont stages; red-cell rupture releases merozoites and causes periodic symptoms. Some parasites differentiate into gametocytes, which are ingested by a mosquito, undergo sexual reproduction, form ookinetes and oocysts, and generate sporozoites that migrate to salivary glands. Prevention includes insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, repellents/protective clothing, removal of breeding sites, prompt diagnosis/treatment, chemoprophylaxis where indicated and vaccination where recommended. A parasite lives in or on a host and obtains benefit at the host's expense. Relationships include parasitism, mutualism, commensalism and other ecological interactions; parasite types include ectoparasites/endoparasites and obligate/facultative forms. Hosts may be definitive, intermediate, paratenic, reservoir, accidental, dead-end or transport hosts.

structured.question: (a) Describe mechanisms by which bacteria resist antimicrobial agents. (b) Outline infection control in a dental unit, hospital waste segregation principles and suitable disinfectants. (c) State characteristics of an ideal antimicrobial agent.
markingGuide: Resistance mechanisms: drug inactivation, target modification, reduced permeability, efflux, bypass pathways/biofilm: 6 marks.
Dental infection control: hand hygiene, PPE, sterilisation, environmental cleaning, safe sharps/waterline practices: 5 marks.
Waste segregation at point of generation, colour coding according to local policy, sharps containers and safe disposal: 4 marks.
Appropriate disinfectant examples and safe use: 3 marks.
Ideal antimicrobial properties: selective toxicity, effective, safe, stable, appropriate spectrum/route: 2 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: Bacteria resist antimicrobials through enzymatic drug inactivation (e.g. beta-lactamases), alteration or protection of drug targets, reduced uptake/permeability, active efflux, metabolic bypass, biofilm formation and acquired resistance genes. Dental infection control includes hand hygiene, PPE, instrument cleaning and validated sterilisation, surface disinfection, safe sharps handling, dental-unit waterline maintenance and appropriate respiratory precautions. Waste should be segregated at the point of generation using current local colour-coding rules; sharps go directly into puncture-resistant containers and infectious waste is handled through approved treatment/disposal. Common surface disinfectant classes include alcohols, chlorine compounds, iodophors, quaternary ammonium compounds and phenolics, selected according to the surface, organism and label instructions. An ideal antimicrobial is selectively toxic, effective at achievable concentrations, safe, stable, practical to administer and has an appropriate spectrum.

structured.question: Define mycology, bacteriology, parasitology, virology, immunology, sterilisation, disinfection and antisepsis. Describe sources of infection and healthcare-associated infection characteristics.
markingGuide: Correct definitions of five microbiology branches: 8 marks.
Distinguishes sterilisation, disinfection and antisepsis: 6 marks.
Four infection sources/reservoirs: 3 marks.
Healthcare-associated infection characteristics/control responsibility: 3 marks.
structured.modelAnswer: Mycology is the study of fungi; bacteriology studies bacteria; parasitology studies parasites; virology studies viruses; immunology studies immune systems and responses. Sterilisation destroys/removes all microbial forms including spores. Disinfection reduces or destroys many pathogens on inanimate objects but may not destroy spores. Antisepsis applies antimicrobial agents to living tissue. Infection sources include humans, animals, soil, water, food, fomites and endogenous flora. Healthcare-associated infections are acquired during care, were not present/incubating at admission, may be linked to procedures/devices or cross-transmission, and are prevented through an institutional infection-prevention programme and committee.
